pages.text: The Baling Talks happened in northern Malaya on 28 and 29 December 1955. They were held to try to stop the Malayan Emergency. The main people there were Tunku Abdul Rahman, David Marshall, and Chin Peng.

pages.text: The Malayan Emergency was a state of emergency declared by the British colonial government in 1948. It lasted until 1960. There was a guerrilla war between government forces and the Malayan National Liberation Army.

Earlier, the government offered an amnesty to the communists on 8 September 1955. However, very few communists surrendered to the authorities. The communists made anti-amnesty propaganda and threatened defectors with severe punishment.

Chin Peng proposed a referendum to the ruling British government and Malayan officials. The meeting wanted a mutual end to the conflict. The Malayan government representatives dismissed all of Chin Peng's demands.

The talks lasted more than eight hours over two days at a school near Baling town. The MCP was represented by Chin Peng, Rashid Maidin, and Chen Tien. The other side had Tunku Abdul Rahman, Dato Tan Cheng-Lock, and David Marshall.

The talks failed because the surrender terms were not acceptable to the Malayan Communist Party. After the talks, the Tunku withdrew the amnesty offer on 8 February 1956 and said the war must be intensified.

pages.text: The Malayan Emergency was a state of emergency declared by the British in 1948 that lasted until 1960. A guerrilla war was fought between government forces and the Malayan National Liberation Army, involving the revocation of many civil rights and special police powers.

In September 1955, the government issued an amnesty declaration to the communists, but few surrendered. The communists had conducted intensive anti-amnesty propaganda within their ranks, tightened discipline, and threatened defectors with severe punishment.

Realizing his struggles had not succeeded, Chin Peng proposed a referendum to the British government and Malayan officials in 1955. The meeting aimed for a mutual end to the conflict, but Malayan representatives led by Tunku Abdul Rahman dismissed all of Chin Peng's demands.

The negotiations began on 28 December 1955 at a school near Baling town and lasted over eight hours across two days. The Communist Party was represented by Chin Peng, Rashid Maidin, and Chen Tien, while the government side included Tunku Abdul Rahman, Dato Tan Cheng-Lock, and David Marshall.

The talks ultimately failed because the surrender terms were unacceptable to the communists. Following the unsuccessful meeting, Tunku Abdul Rahman withdrew the amnesty offer on 8 February 1956, stating that the war must be intensified until one side gave in.

pages.text: The Malayan Emergency spanned from 1948 to 1960 as a state of emergency declared by the British colonial administration. This period involved an insurrection and guerrilla warfare between government forces and the Malayan National Liberation Army, accompanied by the suspension of various civil rights and enhanced police powers.

Prior to the talks, the government issued an amnesty declaration to the communists in September 1955, which yielded very few surrenders. Anticipating the declaration, communist leadership executed intensive internal anti-amnesty propaganda, enforced strict organizational discipline, and threatened potential defectors with severe retribution.

Faced with the stagnation of his campaign, Chin Peng proposed a referendum in 1955 to seek a mutually negotiated end to the conflict alongside British and Malayan officials. However, Malayan representatives headed by Tunku Abdul Rahman summarily dismissed these demands, prompting an escalation in military responses and the deployment of Commonwealth forces.

Convening on 28 December 1955 at a school near Baling town, the sessions spanned over eight hours across two days. The communist delegation comprised Chin Peng, Rashid Maidin, and Chen Tien, whereas the government delegation featured Tunku Abdul Rahman, Dato Tan Cheng-Lock, and David Marshall.

Ultimately, the talks collapsed because the proposed surrender terms were unacceptable to the Malayan Communist Party. Consequently, Tunku Abdul Rahman withdrew the government amnesty offer on 8 February 1956, declaring that the conflict would be intensified until one side conceded.
